# The tests that fail on a GitHub-hosted runner and pass on every lane's machine.
#
# `gate.yml` reads this file to tell **a failure this runner causes** from **a
# failure in the change under test**. Until it existed the workflow could only ask
# *which gate failed*, and answered `the workspace's tests` in both cases — so a
# real broken test and a namespace the runner will not make were the same sentence,
# and the run stayed quiet about both.
#
# # The rules this file lives under
#
# **A line here is an excuse, so it expires.** The workflow checks not only that
# every failure is listed, but that every listed test *still fails*. A test named
# here that passes makes the run say so and is meant to be deleted in the next
# change — otherwise this becomes a list of things nobody is allowed to break,
# which is the opposite of what it is for. Two accessibility-bus tests were on the
# informal version of this list in a comment, and they have passed since the
# compositor and session bus were added to the job; they are not here.
#
# **A line is a statement about the runner, never about the test.** Nothing here
# is skipped, marked `#[ignore]`, or weakened. These tests run on every lane and
# must pass there; `alo/nine-gates` — the status `main` actually requires — is
# posted only from a machine where all of them ran.
#
# **Adding a line is not a way to land a red test.** A failure that is not already
# understood and reproduced does not belong here. Each line below names what was
# measured, and the exit code it produces, so a reader can check the claim.
#
# Format: one test per line, exactly as nextest names it in a FAIL line —
# `<crate>::<binary> <test>`. Blank lines and `#` comments are ignored.

# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
# A network namespace the runner makes but cannot execute the test binary inside
#
# Both of these re-run their own test binary inside a namespace made by
# `unshare --map-root-user --net`, and both fail with the inner shell exiting
# **126** — util-linux's *found, but could not be executed*.
#
# **What is measured, and what is not.** The job's namespace probe runs as root,
# which is how the gates run, and it succeeds at every part of this shape: it makes
# the namespace, runs `ip link set lo up` inside it, execs `/bin/true` inside it,
# and execs a binary from this repository's own tree inside it. The kernel reports
# `apparmor_restrict_unprivileged_userns = 1`, and the same probe as the unprivileged
# `runner` user is refused — but the gates are not that user.
#
# So the usual explanation, that Ubuntu 24.04 blocks unprivileged user namespaces,
# **does not account for this**: root is not blocked, and the probe proves it on
# every run. The cause is not established. It is recorded as unknown rather than
# given a plausible name, because a wrong cause written down is worse than an
# admitted gap — somebody later builds on it. The job's probe now also execs a real
# test binary inside the namespace, which is the measurement that will narrow it.
alo-asking::an_office_that_cannot_connect_still_has_working_ai a_public_address_really_is_unreachable_where_this_is_measured
alo-asking::an_office_that_cannot_connect_still_has_working_ai a_question_bound_for_the_internet_is_told_once_and_truthfully
alo-asking::an_office_that_cannot_connect_still_has_working_ai nothing_on_the_road_addresses_a_single_packet_off_the_network
alo-asking::an_office_that_cannot_connect_still_has_working_ai with_no_route_off_the_network_two_machines_still_find_each_other_pair_ask_and_answer
alo-nearby::asked_and_answered_over_ipv6 asked_and_answered_over_ipv6_as_over_ipv4
